newsitem.title: INDIA: India fire underlines casual approach to safety.
newsitem.headline: India fire underlines casual approach to safety.

text.p: A blaze that engulfed a gathering of Hindu worshippers in eastern India killing at least 182 people has highlighted the country's disregard for fire safety, officials said on Monday.

"It is kind of a casual approach, lack of accountability and no regard for safety," P.S. Das, additional director general of the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), told Reuters in the capital New Delhi. BIS sets national technical standards.
Flames tore through temporary shelters at the Hindu gathering in Baripada town in eastern Orissa state on Sunday, killing at least 182 people and injuring more than 160, police said.

The fire destroyed a cluster of makeshift shelters on the last day of a convention dedicated to a Hindu guru. All the victims were believed to be male. The cause of the fire was thought to be a short circuit or exploding gas cylinder.

The state government has launched an inquiry into what is believed to be the deadliest fire in India since December 1995 when about 425 people died when flames and smoke engulfed a school prize-giving ceremony in the northern town of Dabwali.
India has no federal fire safety regulations. The BIS has recommended a set of rules, but the 26 states are free to adopt or reject them.
"We are a technical body and only recommend the safety standards," said Das.
He said the BIS had written to state governments after the Dabwali fire about the need to adhere to fire safety rules, but the agency had no power to enforce them.
"For implementation of safety, the local authorities are responsible," he said.
After the Dabwali fire, the safety guidelines were circulated to state governments and information was disseminated through the media, officials said.
"People are aware of the hazards but there is no regard for safety regulations," said R.C. Sharma, deputy chief of New Delhi's fire service.
Das said there was only one exit at Dabwali and this created panic that set off a stampede. Authorities said there were few exits in the makeshift shelters in Orissa.
Officials also said local authorities who permitted temporary structures often failed to check the design or types of material.
Sunday's blaze was the most recent in a series of disasters to hit India's Hindu community.
Last July 15, nearly 40 Hindu devotees were killed when scores of worshippers stampeded through a temple complex in the central state of Madhya Pradesh.
On the same day, 21 people were killed and 40 injured when Hindu worshippers rushed to bathe in the Ganges river in the sacred town of Haridwar in northern state of Uttar Pradesh.
A month later, 225 Hindu devotees died in severe cold weather during an annual trek to a holy cave in the Himalayas.
